mainEntity.name: Can I have dental implants if I take blood pressure medication?

acceptedAnswer.text: In many cases, yes — but it depends on the specific medication, the dosage, and how well your blood pressure is managed. Certain antihypertensive drugs can interact with anaesthetics or affect bleeding, and some cause oral side effects such as dry mouth or gum changes. Your dental team will review your medication list during your consultation and may liaise with your GP if needed. Treatment will only proceed when it is considered clinically safe and appropriate for your individual circumstances.

mainEntity.name: What blood pressure reading is considered too high for dental implant surgery?

acceptedAnswer.text: There is no single universal threshold, as clinical decisions are made on a case-by-case basis. As a general guide, many dental clinicians will defer elective surgical procedures if a blood pressure reading is significantly elevated on the day of treatment — for example, above 180/110 mmHg. If this occurs, the dentist may recommend that you consult your GP before rescheduling. Blood pressure can fluctuate, so a single elevated reading does not necessarily mean implants are unsuitable for you long-term.

mainEntity.name: Does hypertension affect how dental implants heal?

acceptedAnswer.text: Well-controlled hypertension does not typically impair the osseointegration process — the way bone fuses with the titanium implant. However, poorly controlled blood pressure, particularly when associated with conditions such as diabetes or compromised circulation, may affect tissue healing. This is one of the reasons that optimising your overall health before implant placement is an important part of the planning process. Your dental team will take your health status into account when assessing the likely success of treatment.

mainEntity.name: Is dental implant surgery painful for patients with high blood pressure?

acceptedAnswer.text: Dental implant placement is carried out under local anaesthesia, so patients do not typically experience pain during the procedure itself. Post-operative discomfort, swelling, and minor bleeding are normal and usually managed with over-the-counter pain relief as advised. For patients with hypertension, the type of anaesthetic used may be adapted to minimise cardiovascular effects. If you experience heightened dental anxiety — which can temporarily elevate blood pressure — speak to your dental team in advance about anxiety management options.

mainEntity.name: Should I tell my GP I am considering dental implants?

acceptedAnswer.text: It is generally advisable to inform your GP if you are considering any elective surgical procedure, including dental implants, particularly if you have a cardiovascular condition like hypertension. Your GP can confirm whether your blood pressure is currently well controlled and advise on any medication considerations. In some cases, your dental team may write to your GP as part of pre-treatment planning. Open communication between your medical and dental providers supports the safest possible care.

mainEntity.name: What should I do if I have high blood pressure and a missing tooth?

acceptedAnswer.text: If you have hypertension and are missing one or more teeth, the first step is to arrange a dental consultation. A qualified dentist can assess your overall oral health, discuss tooth replacement options suitable for your circumstances — which may include implants, bridges, or dentures — and review how your medical history influences treatment planning. There is no need to delay seeking advice simply because you have high blood pressure. A consultation is an opportunity to gather information, not a commitment to any particular treatment path.
